answer.evidence: The stair run is a repeating pattern of 4-5 olive tread rows (top surfaces) that end in a lighter or brown front-edge row. Below each edge sit 2-3 rows of brown riser face and a 1-row dark shadow line (rows 5-7, 13-15, 21-23, 29-31, 37-39, 44-47). Each tread is therefore a horizontal surface with a vertical riser below it, so the steps read as a 3/4 view. The dark cliff walls at the left and right edges are plain vertical faces. Rows 48-63 are flat ground at the foot of the stairs.

styleAnswer.evidence: The candidate is a small stair piece: a dark brown wooden-looking staircase with stepped bands above a flat tan/peat base. The measured facts show 9 visible tones per tile, above the grass (3) and paving (7) references. Only 10% of dark edge pixels are neutral, so the outlines lean brown and read as dark_material_tone. However, 25% of the candidate is near-flat, and the bottom area is a large flat tan fill with no grain, speckle or variation. The steps themselves have only about 3 lightness steps per material (highlight, mid, dark), against the 5-6 steps Beodeul uses. The reference grass and paving have 0% near-flat coverage and carry per-element clumps and individually shaded stones. The flat base and the shallow ramps would look plainer than the references at the same scale, so it fails.

answer.evidence: The stair run is drawn as repeating tread and riser pairs on an 8-row period. Each tread is a 4-5 row olive band (e.g. rows 8-12, 16-20). Each tread ends in a lighter brown front-edge line (rows 13, 21, 29), followed by 2-3 rows of darker brown riser, with a near-black shadow line at the bottom (rows 7, 15, 23, 31, 39, 47). The flat ground below, rows 48-63, is a separate surface. The dark cliff walls on the left and right are vertical faces that flank the stairs.

styleAnswer.evidence: The outline passes: only 10% of dark edge pixels are neutral, and the board shows dark brown beside the wood, so the line is a tinted material tone rather than a sticker outline. The visible-tone count (9 per tile, against 3 for the grass and 7 for the paving) also meets the references. However, the candidate has only 14 distinct colours in total, which gives about 3-4 steps per material against the references' 5-6. The planks are fairly uniform bands with little per-plank grain. The lower tan peat/ground area is one large, almost flat block of a single colour with no dots or grain. This is why 25% of the candidate sits in flat 5x5 blocks, while both references are at 0%. Beodeul ground tiles carry grain across the whole surface, so this flat fill reads as shallow and the piece does not match the references. When in doubt, fail.

answer.evidence: Rows 0-47 repeat a step pattern every 8 rows. Each step has 4-5 rows of olive tread, then a lighter or brown front-edge row (about rows 5, 13, 21), then 2-3 rows of riser and dark eave shadow (rows 6-7, 14-15, 22-23, and so on) that end in a near-black line. That is a top surface with an edge line and shadow, plus a 3-row front face, for each of the six steps. The dark side walls at left and right are the cliff, drawn as vertical faces. Rows 48-63 are a uniform flat ground fill (L=136) at the foot of the stairs. The structure matches the green cabinet reference: top band, edge line, eave shadow, then face.

styleAnswer.evidence: The stair portion is a column of dark-brown-outlined wooden treads with a few highlight and grain dots, and about 4 lightness steps on the wood. Only 10% of its dark edge pixels are neutral, so the outline is tinted dark brown and reads as a material tone, not a sticker line. Measured visible tones per tile (9) are above both references (3 and 7), so the tile count alone does not fail it. However, the whole bottom landing is one flat tan block of well over 5x5 pixels with no grain, speckle or variation. Near-flat coverage is 25%, while both Beodeul references are at 0%. Beodeul ground pieces carry texture across every tile, and this flat peat or sand area reads as a plain fill next to them. The treads are also fairly regular and shallow compared with the 5-6 steps per material in the references. With a quarter of the piece flat and the shading shallower than Beodeul, I fail it when in doubt.

surfaces.part: flat ground apron at the foot of the stairs

answer.evidence: Six stacked steps repeat every 8 rows. Each has a 4-5 row olive tread, then a lighter brown front-edge line (rows 5, 13, 21, 28, 36, 44), then 2-3 rows of dark riser/eave shadow ending in a near-black line (rows 7, 15, 23, 31, 39, 47). The treads are the horizontal top surfaces and the brown/dark bands are the vertical risers, so the stairs read as a 3/4 climb to the north. The dark strips at the left and right edges are cliff wall flanking the cut, not a receding side face. Rows 48-63 are a flat uniform ground apron.

styleAnswer.evidence: The candidate is a narrow staircase (about 4 tiles tall, 2 wide) of brown wooden steps with a flat tan/sand patch at the bottom. Its dark edges are tinted brown (only 10% near-neutral), so the outline is dark material tone and not a sticker line. Each step has a highlight, a mid tone and a dark riser, plus some speckle, so the stairs show about 4 shading steps against the references' 5-6. The 9 visible tones per tile are above the grass reference (3) and the paving reference (7). Weaknesses: the sand area at the bottom is a large flat fill with no grain, and the 25% near-flat coverage is well above the references' 0%. The side rails and the step faces are also fairly uniform, so the piece is thinner in craft than the stone-by-stone paving. The flat sand patch and the shallower ramps keep it below the Beodeul standard, so on balance it fails.
